articles.title: ‘Evil Genius’ Review: Courteney Cox Fashions the Pizza Bomber Case Into a Broad, Shrilly Played Farce
articles.summary: If you were glued to “Evil Genius,” Netflix’s 2018 documentary series about the bizarre “pizza bomber” killing of 2003, but wished its true-crime study rang just a little less true, then Courteney Cox’s new film of the same title has you covered.
body: Sharing its title with Netflix’s hit 2018 documentary series, this slipshod vehicle for Patricia Arquette and David Harbour embellishes the facts with comedy, but not much humanity.

The core details of the case are presented much as they were in the doc series and copious headlines before it. On August 28, 2003, middle-aged pizza deliverer Brian Wells (played by actor-filmmaker Tom McCarthy as a hopeless patsy) robbed a branch of PNC Bank outside Erie, Pennsylvania, claiming to be a hostage, with an explosive device collared to his neck that he said would be detonated if his demands were not met. Demanding $250,000 but making off with a four-figure sum, he was apprehended shortly afterwards by police, whereupon the bomb did indeed go off, killing him, and cuing a tortuous, years-long FBI investigation.

articles.title: Rei Ami on Her New Pop Girl Era, and How Feeling Confident Inspired Her New Single ‘2 Loud’: ‘It’s a Clapback’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Rei Ami is loving life, and she’s also learned to love herself. But it wasn’t an easy journey getting to this stage. Before breaking out as one-third of Huntr/x in Netflix’s smash “KPop Demon Hunters,” Ami largely released rap songs like “Snow Cone” and “Body Bag,” which she says came from a place…
body: “2 Loud” signals a shift in her music, influenced by Ami’s inner pop girl. Here, Ami speaks with Variety about this new chapter and sound, and what to expect from her in the near future.

We’ve chatted so many times. You saw me and the girls throughout the campaign, and it was crazy. I’ve never been thrust into that level of visibility in my life. I’ve never had people online comment about just me existing. And I had to process so many things all at once. I’ve had to develop new habits, like not reading the comments and putting a pause on the doomscrolling.

At one point, I read a comment about one of our performances, and it said, “She’s doing too much.” I thought, “How am I doing too much?” I am in a position where millions of people are watching me. I have an opportunity of a lifetime. You want me to not do my job, right? What are you even talking about?

And it made me think: These people don’t actually know me. Sometimes, you just have to let it be. You don’t have to understand why they would comment such a bizarre thing, but they do, and that’s not my problem.

articles.title: Why stop at Wuthering Heights: House of the Damned? Bring on Mrs Dalloway’s Rampage!
articles.summary: It isn’t just Winnie the Pooh – now the star of Blood & Honey II. Budget shockers are treating any story with expired copyright as ripe for murderous exploitation. It is significant that, at this point in our cultural journey, we have become accustomed to film producers jumping on every single…
body: But if you zoom out even a tiny amount, it all starts to look a little silly. Not because it suggests the paying public has a fondness for inarguably bad horror films based on loose interpretations of recognisable figures, but because it’s missing the bigger picture. In other words, while producers are watching eagerly for the next newly out-of-copyright property to exploit (by the way, Babar the Elephant will enter the public domain in January), there is an entire ocean of public domain work just sitting there to be desecrated.

In which case, you really have to applaud whoever came up with the idea of Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned. Available on digital platforms in three short weeks (on 19 October in fact), it is a remake of Emily Brontë’s classic novel, only scarier. In the film, as far as I am able to tell, Cathy has died and her ghost starts haunting Heathcliff to the point that he starts murdering everyone. Is it any good? All signs point to not really, especially since the trailer contains a shot where Cathy seems to become a zombie so that she can punch through a window and strangle someone to death. But will I watch it? Oh God, try to stop me.

articles.title: Marooned Lord Byron statue returns to Hyde Park
articles.summary: The statue was left isolated on a Park Lane traffic island after new roads were built in the 1960s.
body: A statue of the 19th-century poet Lord Byron has been returned to Hyde Park, nearly 70 years after it was isolated on a traffic island when new roads were built through the area in the early 1960s.

The Grade II-listed statue was erected as a national memorial in 1880 after receiving special permission from Queen Victoria. Changes to the Park Lane road layout 80 years later left it inaccessible, leading it to become isolated, neglected and dirty.
The Lord Byron Society launched a campaign to relocate the statue six years ago, arguing it had become neglected.
The move cost more than £400,000, funded by a £230,000 grant from The National Lottery Heritage Fund and additional donations.
points: The statue was left isolated on a Park Lane traffic island after new roads were built in the 1960s.

articles.title: Homer Gere Shares His Theory About ‘The Shards’ and Robert Mallory
articles.summary: As the Ryan Murphy adaptation of Bret Ellis Easton's classic novel awaits a season two renewal, Gere dives into the season one ending and what it means for the show and his career.
body: “You can’t understand him because, in my opinion, he’s not real,” says the actor who plays the mysterious character in Ryan Murphy ‘s adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis ‘ classic novel, which recently concluded its nine-episode first season.

The season one finale of The Shards ended on a cliffhanger by design. Creator Murphy, who has taken liberties from the source material, and Ellis have plans to turn the show into a three- or four-season offering. So as Gere and the audience await official news on a season two renewal, The Hollywood Reporter spoke with the breakout actor, and son to Richard Gere, about his theories for the show (like why he thinks Robert is definitely not the killer) and how his first major role is changing his life: “I’m feeling pretty good. I’m happy to be here.”
The Shards is now streaming its finale and all of season one on Hulu. Head here for THR ‘s show coverage.

articles.title: Mellody Hobson Departs Embattled L.A. Olympics Board Ahead of Lucas Museum Opening (Exclusive)
articles.summary: The Fair Games Coalition, a local activist group, has targeted the Lucas Museum with protests over Hobson's oversight of the 2028 Olympics organizing committee.
body: Mellody Hobson, the prominent business executive and wife of George Lucas, has resigned from the board of L.A.’s embattled 2028 Olympic Games organizing committee, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.

Hobson and the committee, known as LA28, didn’t respond to THR. The Lucas Museum, where she is co-founder, opens to the public on Sept. 22, following a series of opening events. LA28 has been navigating a well-publicized cycle of financial, logistical and political challenges. These include a backlash over ticket prices, security costs and transportation issues, as well as sports-entertainment mogul Casey Wasserman’s continued board chairmanship following revelations of his relationship with convicted child sex trafficker Ghislaine Maxwell — even as he’s been forced to relinquish his stake in his namesake management company, which has since rebranded.

articles.title: ‘When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true’: the incredible journey behind The Cycle of Love
articles.summary: Documentary director Orlando von Einsiedel on how the real life tale of a man who cycles 6,000 miles from India to Sweden to find his true love will warm your heart. New Delhi, December 1975.
body: New Delhi, December 1975. It was love at first sight when a Swedish hippy called Lotta von Schedvin sat down to be sketched by an Indian street artist, Pradyumna Kumar Mahanandia, known to everyone as PK. In the 10 minutes it took PK to complete her portrait, everything clicked into place for the pair. They were swept headlong in a whirlwind romance, and PK took Lotta to his village in the east of India to meet his family. But soon after, the time came for Lotta to pack up her VW campervan and head back home with her friends.

Heart-stricken PK promised to follow, but a plane ticket to Sweden was an impossible dream. Determined not to lose the love of his life, PK bought a secondhand Raleigh bike, and with $80 sewn into the waistband of his trousers, set off to cycle 6,000 miles to Lotta. He knew the sun set in the west, so that was the direction he took. His plan was to follow the hippy trail, cycling through India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, crossing Europe, finally arriving in Sweden.

articles.title: Neil LaBute and Gia Crovatin on Making Hitchcock-Lean Indie Horror-Comedy ‘Murderous’
articles.summary: LaBute and his creative and real-life partner Gia Crovatin on shooting their shoestring thriller in 10 days, and why he'd rather divide audiences than bore them.
body: Neil LaBute has spent three decades toggling between critical acclaim and heated controversy.

The playwright burst onto the film scene with two sharply observed indie darlings — In the Company of Men (1997) and Your Friends & Neighbors (1998) — that earned festival buzz and positioned him as a fearless voice in contemporary drama, while also labeling him a misogynist, mainly because of the horrible words he put into his male characters’ mouths.

His high-profile attempt to remake The Wicker Man, however, underscored the risk of big-studio ventures. The film, that meme-ably landed Nicolas Cage in a bee-tormented nightmare, was mercilessly dissected by purist fans of the 1973 original. “If I realized then how precious The Wicker Man was to the world of horror, I might never stepped in that arena,” he says now.
